question: What is CQRS pattern?

options.option_value: One model serving reads and writes
Reads and writes served by separate models
No separation between the two paths
A separation living only in the database

answer_explanation: CQRS separates read and write operations to different models for optimization.

question: What is event sourcing pattern?

options.option_value: Keeping only the latest state on record
Keeping every change as an event log
Keeping no record of the state at all
Keeping periodic snapshots and nothing else

answer_explanation: Event Sourcing stores changes as events, reconstructs state by replaying events.

question: What is saga pattern?

options.option_value: One transaction spanning every service
A sequence of steps with compensations
No transactional guarantees whatsoever
A transaction confined to one service

answer_explanation: Saga manages distributed transaction as sequence of local transactions with compensation.

question: What is outbox pattern?

options.option_value: Publishing straight after the commit
Writing the row and message in one commit
Publishing without any durable record
Recording what has already been consumed

answer_explanation: Outbox pattern ensures atomic database update and message publishing.

question: What is inbox pattern?

options.option_value: Handling each message as it arrives
Recording ids so repeats are ignored
Handling no messages whatsoever
Writing the row and message together

answer_explanation: Inbox pattern ensures idempotent message processing with deduplication.

question: What is circuit breaker pattern?

options.option_value: Every call goes straight through
Failing fast once a dependency is sick
Retrying for ever until it succeeds
Waiting indefinitely for a reply

answer_explanation: Circuit breaker stops calls to failing service, returning error immediately.

question: What is retry pattern?

options.option_value: Trying an operation exactly once
Trying a failed operation again
Never attempting an operation twice
Trying for ever without ever stopping

answer_explanation: Retry pattern retries failed operations with backoff for transient failures.

question: What is bulkhead pattern?

options.option_value: One shared pool serving every caller
Separate pools so one failure stays put
Every caller sharing the same resources
No isolation between callers at all

answer_explanation: Bulkhead isolates resources so failure in one doesn't exhaust others.

question: What is timeout pattern?

options.option_value: Waiting indefinitely for a reply
Capping how long a call may wait
Never waiting for a reply at all
Giving up before the call is sent

answer_explanation: Timeout pattern sets upper bound on operation wait time.

question: What is fallback pattern?

options.option_value: Nothing is offered when it fails
Serving something lesser when it fails
Retrying and nothing more than that
Timing out and nothing more than that

answer_explanation: Fallback provides alternative response when primary service fails.

question: What is cache-aside pattern?

options.option_value: The store writes through to the cache
The caller fills the cache on a miss
The cache fetches on a miss itself
Writes go to the cache and drain later

answer_explanation: Cache-aside: application checks cache, loads from DB on miss, populates cache.

question: What is read-through pattern?

options.option_value: The caller fills the cache on a miss
The cache fetches on a miss itself
The store writes through to the cache
Writes go to the cache and drain later

answer_explanation: Read-through: cache library automatically loads from backing store on miss.

question: What is write-through pattern?

options.option_value: Writes go to the cache and drain later
Writes land in cache and store together
The caller fills the cache on a miss
The cache fetches on a miss itself

answer_explanation: Write-through: data written to cache and backing store synchronously.

question: What is write-behind pattern?

options.option_value: Writes land in cache and store together
Writes hit the cache and drain later
No writes reach the store at any point
The store is only ever read from

answer_explanation: Write-behind: written to cache immediately, asynchronously to backing store.

question: What is cache invalidation?

options.option_value: Stale entries are simply left in place
Dropping entries that have gone stale
Adding fresh entries to the cache
No cache is involved in the first place

answer_explanation: Cache invalidation removes stale data to ensure consistency with source.

question: What is time-based cache expiration?

options.option_value: Entries are kept in the cache for ever
Entries lapse after a set period
Entries lapse the moment they are stored
No cache is involved in the first place

answer_explanation: Time-based expiration removes entries after specified time-to-live (TTL).

question: What is write-invalidation?

options.option_value: Stale entries are simply left in place
Dropping the entry when the row changes
Dropping the entry when it is read
No writes ever reach the store

answer_explanation: Write-invalidation removes or updates cache entries when underlying data changes.

question: What is memoization?

options.option_value: Nothing is remembered between calls
Keeping results so they are not recomputed
Caching rows read from the database
Caching responses at the network edge

answer_explanation: Memoization caches function results for given inputs to avoid repeated computation.

question: What is object pool pattern?

options.option_value: Building a fresh one on every request
Handing back objects that cost a lot
No reuse takes place at any point
Exactly one instance ever exists

answer_explanation: Object pool reuses expensive objects (DB connections, threads) instead of recreating.

question: What is connection pool?

options.option_value: A single connection shared by everyone
A set of connections handed out and back
No connection is reused at any point
A fresh connection for every statement

answer_explanation: Connection pool maintains reusable database connections to reduce overhead.

question: What is thread pool?

options.option_value: A single thread handling every task
A set of workers handed queued tasks
No threading is involved at any point
A set of separate operating processes

answer_explanation: Thread pool maintains pool of worker threads to execute submitted tasks.

question: What is worker pool pattern?

options.option_value: A single worker handling every task
Several workers drawing from one queue
No workers are involved at any point
The main thread doing all of the work

answer_explanation: Worker pool: multiple workers process tasks from shared queue concurrently.

question: What is leader election pattern?

options.option_value: No instance ever takes the lead
One instance is chosen to coordinate
Every instance leads at the same time
An instance is picked at random each time

answer_explanation: Leader election selects one instance as coordinator for distributed tasks.

question: What is sharding pattern?

options.option_value: One store holding all of the data
Data split across several stores
Copies of the data on several servers
No splitting takes place at all

answer_explanation: Sharding splits data horizontally across multiple databases based on shard key.

question: What is replication pattern?

options.option_value: One copy of the data and no more
Copies of the data on several servers
Data split across several stores
No copies are made at any point

answer_explanation: Replication copies data to multiple servers for read scaling and availability.

question: What is read replica pattern?

options.option_value: Writes are sent to every server
Reads hit copies, writes hit the primary
Reads and writes both hit the primary
No copies exist to read from

answer_explanation: Read replica: write to primary, read from replicas to distribute load.

question: What is multi-master replication?

options.option_value: Only one server ever accepts writes
Several servers all accept writes
Copies exist but are read-only
No copying takes place at all

answer_explanation: Multi-master replication: multiple servers accept writes, replicate to each other.

question: What is CQRS with event sourcing?

options.option_value: Reads and writes served by one model
Split models over an append-only event log
No events are recorded at any point
Split models with no event log at all

answer_explanation: CQRS with Event Sourcing: separate models, write model stored as events.

question: What is materialized view pattern?

options.option_value: A query stored under a friendly name
A query whose result is stored ahead
No view is defined at any point
A view computed fresh on each read

answer_explanation: Materialized view stores precomputed query results for faster reads.

question: What is index table pattern?

options.option_value: No index is built at any point
Indexes built for the common lookups
Every query scans the table in full
No table is involved in the first place

answer_explanation: Index table creates indexes on frequently queried fields for performance.

question: What is data partitioning?

options.option_value: All the data kept in one place
Data broken up into smaller pieces
No breaking up takes place at all
Data assigned to pieces at random

answer_explanation: Data partitioning divides large dataset into smaller, manageable pieces.

question: What is vertical partitioning?

options.option_value: Splitting the table across its rows
Splitting the table across its columns
No splitting takes place at all
Rows assigned to pieces at random

answer_explanation: Vertical partitioning splits table by columns into separate tables.

question: What is horizontal partitioning?

options.option_value: Splitting the table across its columns
Splitting the table across its rows
No splitting takes place at all
Rows assigned to pieces at random

answer_explanation: Horizontal partitioning (sharding) splits table by rows across multiple tables.

question: What is functional partitioning?

options.option_value: Rows assigned to pieces at random
Splitting by business capability
Splitting on a range of key values
Splitting on a hash of the key

answer_explanation: Functional partitioning splits by business function (users, orders, products).

question: What is strangler fig pattern?

options.option_value: Replacing the whole system in one go
Replacing it one piece at a time
Leaving the old system entirely alone
Rewriting every line from scratch

answer_explanation: Strangler fig incrementally replaces legacy system with new components.

question: What is anti-corruption layer pattern?

options.option_value: Calling the legacy system directly
A translating layer between old and new
No layer sits between the two systems
Rewriting the legacy system entirely

answer_explanation: Anti-corruption layer isolates new system from legacy system semantics.

question: What is gateway pattern?

options.option_value: Outsiders reach each service directly
One doorway for everything outside
No doorway is defined at any point
Many separate doorways, one per client

answer_explanation: Gateway provides single entry point for external systems to access internal services.

question: What is API gateway pattern?

options.option_value: Clients call each service directly
One doorway for every client request
No doorway is defined at any point
One doorway for each service instead

answer_explanation: API gateway is single entry point handling routing, auth, rate limiting.

question: What is backend-for-frontend pattern?

options.option_value: One backend serving every client type
One backend tailored to each client type
No backend is involved at any point
One frontend serving every backend

answer_explanation: BFF creates dedicated backend optimized for specific frontend needs.

question: What is aggregator pattern?

options.option_value: The client calls each service itself
One service combining several replies
No combining takes place at all
Only one service is ever consulted

answer_explanation: Aggregator pattern combines data from multiple services into single response.

question: What is proxy pattern in microservices?

options.option_value: Callers reach the service directly
A stand-in controlling access to it
No stand-in sits in front of it
Every call is made without a hop

answer_explanation: Proxy controls access to service, adding cross-cutting concerns.

question: What is sidecar pattern?

options.option_value: One container doing all of the work
A helper container beside the main one
The main container running on its own
A container that runs before the others

answer_explanation: Sidecar deploys helper container (logging, monitoring) alongside main container.

question: What is ambassador pattern?

options.option_value: Each service calls out for itself
A local proxy owning outbound calls
No proxy is involved at any point
Every call goes out over one socket

answer_explanation: Ambassador is proxy handling routing, circuit breaking, retry for service.

question: What is scatter-gather pattern?

options.option_value: One service answers the whole request
Many asked at once, replies combined
No fan-out takes place at any point
Only one service is ever consulted

answer_explanation: Scatter-gather sends request to multiple services, aggregates responses.

question: What is queue-based load leveling?

options.option_value: Callers hit the service directly
A queue absorbing bursts of traffic
No queue is involved at any point
Every call is handled synchronously

answer_explanation: Queue-based load leveling buffers work in queue to handle load spikes.

question: What is competing consumers pattern?

options.option_value: One consumer draining the whole queue
Several consumers sharing one queue
No consumers are involved at all
One queue serving one producer only

answer_explanation: Competing consumers: multiple consumers process messages from same queue.

question: What is priority queue pattern?

options.option_value: Messages served in arrival order
Messages served by importance first
Messages served newest-first instead
Messages served in a random order

answer_explanation: Priority queue processes higher priority messages before lower priority.

question: What is scheduler agent supervisor pattern?

options.option_value: Work is run the instant it arrives
Work scheduled, watched and retried
No scheduling takes place at all
Work is run without any supervision

answer_explanation: Scheduler Agent Supervisor schedules tasks, monitors execution, handles failures.

question: What is compute resource consolidation pattern?

options.option_value: Each task given a machine of its own
Several tasks packed onto one machine
No packing takes place at any point
As many machines as can be obtained

answer_explanation: Compute resource consolidation combines multiple tasks to single compute unit.

question: What is valet key pattern?

options.option_value: The client is handed full access
The client is handed a scoped token
The client is given no access at all
The client is handed the master key

answer_explanation: Valet key gives clients time-limited, restricted direct access to resources.

question: What is claim check pattern?

options.option_value: The whole payload rides the queue
The payload is stored, a pointer sent
No message is sent at any point
The payload is duplicated on the queue

answer_explanation: Claim check stores large payload, sends small reference through messaging system.

question: What is sequential convoy pattern?

options.option_value: Related messages need no ordering
Related messages handled in order
Messages handled in random order
No messages are handled at all

answer_explanation: Sequential convoy processes set of related messages in order, not concurrently.

question: What is choreography pattern?

options.option_value: One coordinator drives every step
Each service reacts to events itself
Nothing coordinates the steps at all
Every step is made a blocking call

answer_explanation: Choreography: services publish and subscribe to events, no central controller.

question: What is orchestration pattern?

options.option_value: Each service reacts to events itself
One coordinator drives every step
Nothing coordinates the steps at all
Only events may drive the workflow

answer_explanation: Orchestration: central coordinator directs participants through workflow.

question: What is compensating transaction pattern?

options.option_value: A step that carries the work forward
A step that undoes an earlier one
Nothing is ever undone at any point
A step that only reads existing data

answer_explanation: Compensating transaction undoes changes made by completed transaction.

question: What is database per service pattern?

options.option_value: Every service shares one store
Each service owns its own store
One store is shared by the whole system
No store is involved at any point

answer_explanation: Database per Service: each microservice has its own private database.

question: What is shared database anti-pattern?

options.option_value: A practice worth reaching for
Several services writing one store
The approach usually recommended
The approach the pattern prescribes

answer_explanation: Shared database is anti-pattern: services become tightly coupled.

question: What is saga orchestration pattern?

options.option_value: Each participant reacts to events
One coordinator drives every step
Nothing coordinates the steps at all
One transaction spans every service

answer_explanation: Saga orchestration: central coordinator directs saga participants.

question: What is saga choreography pattern?

options.option_value: One coordinator drives every step
Each participant reacts to events
Nothing coordinates the steps at all
One transaction spans every service

answer_explanation: Saga choreography: participants publish events, others subscribe and react.

question: What is API composition pattern?

options.option_value: One service answers the whole call
Several replies combined for the client
No combining takes place at all
The client calls each service itself

answer_explanation: API composition combines data from multiple services for client.

question: What is command-side in CQRS?

options.option_value: Read operations
Write operations
Both
Neither

answer_explanation: Command-side in CQRS handles write operations and business logic.

question: What is query-side in CQRS?

options.option_value: Write operations
Read operations
Both
Neither

answer_explanation: Query-side in CQRS handles read operations, optimized for queries.

question: What is event in event sourcing?

options.option_value: The state exactly as it stands now
An unchangeable record of what happened
A record that may be edited afterwards
No record is written at any point at all

answer_explanation: Event is immutable record of something that happened in the past.

question: What is event store?

options.option_value: A store for structured relational rows
A store tuned for append-only events
A store for frequently read values
A tree of directories holding files

answer_explanation: Event store is specialized database for storing and querying events.

question: What is aggregate in DDD?

options.option_value: A single entity standing on its own
A cluster of entities treated as a unit
A table stored in the database
A stateless component holding logic

answer_explanation: Aggregate is cluster of domain objects treated as single unit for data changes.

question: What is aggregate root?

options.option_value: Whichever entity you happen to hold
The one entity the cluster is reached by
An object defined purely by its values
A stateless component holding logic

answer_explanation: Aggregate root is only entity outside objects can hold reference to.

question: What is domain event?

options.option_value: Something the user clicked on screen
Something meaningful that happened
Something a database trigger recorded
Something observed on the network

answer_explanation: Domain event is something that happened in domain that domain experts care about.

question: What is event handler?

options.option_value: The code that raises the event
The code that reacts to the event
The store the events are kept in
No such code exists in the design

answer_explanation: Event handler is code that executes in response to domain event.

question: What is event projector?

options.option_value: The code that raises the event itself
Code building a read model from events
The store where the events are kept
The code that handles an incoming command

answer_explanation: Event projector (read model projector) creates read model from stream of events.

question: What is snapshot in event sourcing?

options.option_value: The full log of every event so far
A periodic save of the current state
No saving takes place at any point
Replaying every event from the start

answer_explanation: Snapshot saves aggregate state at point in time to reduce event replay.

question: What is optimistic concurrency control?

options.option_value: Holding a lock for the whole transaction
Spotting the clash when you commit
No control is applied at any point
Holding a lock before reading anything

answer_explanation: Optimistic concurrency: detect conflicts when saving, retry if needed.

question: What is pessimistic concurrency control?

options.option_value: No lock is taken at any point at all
Holding a lock for the whole transaction
Spotting the clash only when you commit
No control is applied at any point at all

answer_explanation: Pessimistic concurrency: lock resources when reading to prevent conflicts.

question: What is versioning in event sourcing?

options.option_value: Event shapes are fixed for ever
Coping with events whose shape changed
Only one shape is ever supported
No events are stored in the first place

answer_explanation: Event versioning handles changes to event schema over time.

question: What is upcasting in event sourcing?

options.option_value: Rewriting new events into the old shape
Rewriting old events into the new shape
No rewriting takes place at any point
Deleting events that no longer fit

answer_explanation: Upcasting transforms old event versions to current schema when reading.

question: What is event migration?

options.option_value: No rewriting takes place at any point
Rewriting stored events into a new shape
Appending brand-new events to the log
No events are stored in the first place

answer_explanation: Event migration transforms stored events when schema changes significantly.

question: What is two-phase commit?

options.option_value: Everyone commits in a single step
Everyone prepares, then all commit or abort
Nothing coordinates the participants
Participants commit whenever they like

answer_explanation: Two-phase commit ensures atomic transaction across multiple resources.

question: What is SAGA vs 2PC?

options.option_value: The two approaches are the same
Saga compensates; 2PC is atomic
2PC is the better choice in every case
Saga blocks until every step finishes

answer_explanation: Saga is long-running transaction with compensation; 2PC is atomic commit protocol.

question: What is eventual consistency?

options.option_value: Every reader sees the write at once
Readers converge on the value in time
Every reader always sees the latest write
Readers never converge on one value

answer_explanation: Eventual consistency: replicas converge to same value if no new updates.

question: What is strong consistency?

options.option_value: Readers converge on the value in time
Every reader sees the latest write
Readers may see arbitrarily stale data
Readers never converge on one value

answer_explanation: Strong consistency: all nodes see same data at same time.

question: What is BASE in distributed systems?

options.option_value: The strict transactional guarantees only
Basically available, soft state, eventual
The name of one particular database
A category of database transaction only

answer_explanation: BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency (vs ACID).

question: What is CAP theorem?

options.option_value: A result about raw throughput limits
Consistency, availability, partitions: pick two
A result about cryptographic strength only
A result about how far a system can scale

answer_explanation: CAP: in distributed system, can only guarantee two of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance.

question: What is PACELC theorem?

options.option_value: Simply another name for CAP
CAP extended with a latency trade-off
A result about cryptographic strength
A result about throughput limits

answer_explanation: PACELC extends CAP: if partitioned, choose availability/consistency; else latency/consistency.

question: What is idempotent consumer?

options.option_value: Each delivery has a fresh effect
Repeat deliveries leave the same result
No such property is guaranteed here
Each message is handled exactly once

answer_explanation: Idempotent consumer: processing same message multiple times has same effect as once.

question: What is message deduplication?

options.option_value: Repeats are handled like any other
Spotting repeats and dropping them
No such handling takes place here
Only one message is ever sent

answer_explanation: Message deduplication ensures duplicate messages are not processed multiple times.

question: What is exactly-once semantics?

options.option_value: Every message arrives one or more times
Every message takes effect exactly once
Every message arrives zero or one times
Nothing at all is guaranteed here

answer_explanation: Exactly-once semantics ensure message is processed exactly one time despite failures.

question: What is at-least-once semantics?

options.option_value: Every message arrives exactly once
Every message arrives one or more times
Every message arrives zero or one times
Messages may never arrive at all

answer_explanation: At-least-once: message delivered, but possible duplicates.

question: What is at-most-once semantics?

options.option_value: Every message arrives exactly once
Every message arrives zero or one times
Every message arrives one or more times
Messages may never arrive at all

answer_explanation: At-most-once: no duplicates possible, but message may be lost.

question: What is distributed transaction?

options.option_value: A transaction inside one single store
A transaction spanning several stores
A transaction confined to one process
No transaction is involved at all

answer_explanation: Distributed transaction spans multiple databases or services.

question: What is TCC (Try-Confirm-Cancel)?

options.option_value: Everyone prepares, then all commit
Try reserves, confirm commits, cancel frees
A sequence of steps with compensations
No particular structure is imposed

answer_explanation: TCC: Try reserves resources, Confirm commits, Cancel releases reservations.

question: What is SAGA execution coordinator?

options.option_value: Nothing coordinates the steps at all
The component driving the whole saga
A store for structured relational rows
A buffer holding messages until read

answer_explanation: Saga Execution Coordinator manages saga execution and compensation.

question: What is process manager in sagas?

options.option_value: Nothing routes the messages at all
The component routing saga messages
A store for structured relational rows
A store tuned for append-only events

answer_explanation: Process Manager (Routing Slip) centralizes saga logic, routes messages to next step.

question: What is timeout in sagas?

options.option_value: A step may run for as long as it likes
A cap on how long a step may take
Steps are never given any time limit
No saga is involved in the first place

answer_explanation: Timeout limits how long saga waits for step completion before compensation.

question: What is compensation in sagas?

options.option_value: A step that carries the work forward
A step that undoes an earlier one
Nothing is ever undone at any point
A step that only reads existing data

answer_explanation: Compensating transaction undoes changes made by completed saga step.

question: What is semantic lock?

options.option_value: A row lock taken in the database
A flag the application checks itself
No lock is taken at any point
A lock held for the whole transaction

answer_explanation: Semantic lock (reserved state) prevents saga from seeing inconsistent intermediate state.

question: What is commutative updates?

options.option_value: The order they are applied matters
They may be applied in any order
No updates are applied at any point
They must be applied one after another

answer_explanation: Commutative updates produce same result regardless of execution order.

question: What is pessimistic view in sagas?

options.option_value: Steps are left in their natural order
Steps reordered to shrink the risk window
No reordering takes place at all
Steps are run in a random order

answer_explanation: Pessimistic view reorders saga steps to minimize business risk from conflicts.

question: What is value-based concurrency?

options.option_value: Clashes are prevented by taking locks
Clashes spotted by comparing values
No concurrency is permitted at all
Clashes spotted by comparing timestamps

answer_explanation: Value-based concurrency detects conflicts by comparing before and after values.
